title: Sensitive Info Goes Into ‘No Reply’ Emails Constantly. This Guy Sees It All
gist: Security researcher Cory Solovewicz bought the domains noreply.us and noreply.net and set them as catch-all inboxes, accidentally collecting ~440,000 automated corporate emails containing injury reports, credentials, order confirmations and other private data that senders assumed went nowhere. A second researcher, Mike Sheward, replicated the effect with deleteduser.com for about $15; both now defensively hoard 30+ such domains because the same trick is trivially available to criminals or nation-states.

insights.claim: Placeholder email domains such as noreply.us, noreply.net and deleteduser.com are ordinary registrable domains, so anyone who buys one and configures a catch-all inbox silently receives the automated mail that corporate systems send to those addresses.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A near-zero-cost attack surface that no security budget covers — data-loss and email-hygiene vendors have an unaddressed market, and any enterprise using placeholder domains it does not own is exfiltrating data by default.
insights.locator: Solovewicz is receiving the avalanche of messages

insights.claim: Companies route mail to placeholder domains believing the messages go nowhere and cannot be monitored, and often rewrite a departing employee's address to a placeholder domain instead of deleting the account outright.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Identity/offboarding tooling is the root cause — HR-IT deprovisioning workflows, not email security, are where the fix and the spend belong.
insights.quote: companies appear to be simply changing email addresses rather than entirely deleting accounts from their systems
insights.locator: Earlier this year, Mike Sheward, the head of security at EV charging company Xeal

insights.claim: Every message arriving at these catch-all domains is machine-generated by corporate systems rather than written by humans, which means the leak is a systemic configuration defect rather than individual user error.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Systemic defects scale and persist — expect the volume to keep growing until platform vendors change defaults, not until users are retrained.
insights.quote: The messages are automated by company systems, not written by humans, the researcher says.
insights.locator: Overall, emails have been sent from more than 14,000 “from” addresses

insights.claim: One of Cory Solovewicz's domains has registered 401,796 inbound messages since December 2024, an average of 699.99 messages per day.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Quantifies a leak channel most CISOs have never measured; a single hobbyist domain sees ~700 misdirected corporate emails a day.
insights.quote: one of the domains at which the security researcher receives email has registered 401,796 messages—by his calculations that’s an average of 699.99 pings per day
insights.locator: Cory Solovewicz receives more unwanted emails than you

insights.claim: The noreply.net domain has taken in roughly 400,000 messages in eighteen months, 28,365 of them carrying file attachments, while noreply.us has taken 37,255 messages across 2,345 days.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Attachment-bearing mail is the high-value tail — nearly 30,000 documents left the sending organizations' control on one domain alone.
insights.locator: Solovewicz says that the noreply.net domain is the largest he owns

insights.claim: Mail to the two noreply domains has originated from more than 14,000 distinct 'from' addresses spanning 6,200 root domains, indicating the misconfiguration is spread across thousands of independent organizations rather than concentrated in a few bad actors.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Breadth this wide means no single vendor patch fixes it — the remediation market is long-tail consulting and auditing, not a product sale.
insights.quote: Overall, emails have been sent from more than 14,000 “from” addresses, from 6,200 root domains.
insights.locator: Over the month before his conference talk

insights.claim: A probe scanning 7,136 candidate placeholder domains found 328 already configured with catch-all inboxes, meaning hundreds of other collection points for misdirected corporate mail already exist in unknown hands.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: The 328 known catch-alls are the measurable floor of an unmeasured problem — assume adversarial collection is already running at scale.
insights.quote: I’ve scanned 7,136 domains, and 328 of them were identified as having catch-all inboxes configured
insights.locator: As part of his Defcon talk

insights.claim: Material received at these domains includes injury reports from a city government, test platform credentials, service and repair orders, school platform account-setup emails, and pizza order confirmations — a mix of PII, operational data and live secrets.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Leaked test credentials are directly weaponizable; the rest is extortion-grade PII, so the exposure is both breach risk and regulatory risk.
insights.quote: I get service orders for people that need repairs. I get lots of test platform credentials
insights.locator: This deluge isn’t the regular flood of spam

insights.claim: Mike Sheward's placeholder domains have received Viagra order details, work vacation approval requests, hotel bookings with full names, and Zoom meeting invitations from a UK government agency, with cybersecurity firms and Microsoft partner companies among the frequent senders.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Security vendors and government agencies leaking through the same channel undercuts the assumption that mature buyers have this covered.
insights.locator: Like Solovewicz, Sheward has seen thousands of unintended emails

insights.claim: One of the heaviest senders to Sheward's domains is an AI company using object-recognition to detect safety-protocol violations by workers at Middle East industrial sites, which has pushed thousands of CCTV stills to a stranger's inbox.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Computer-vision surveillance deployments inherit all the sloppy email plumbing of ordinary SaaS — a live liability vector for the industrial-AI category.
insights.locator: One of the most frequent sources of email

insights.claim: The placeholder-domain leak is not new: nearly twenty years ago Brian Krebs, then at the Washington Post, documented companies sending millions of messages to @donotreply.com addresses, meaning two decades of disclosure has not changed engineering defaults.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Twenty years of non-remediation is the base rate — bet against voluntary industry fixes and in favor of the problem persisting through the next tech cycle.
insights.locator: While the issue is not a new one

insights.claim: The failure is trivially preventable because organizations can send placeholder mail to internal domains or to the reserved .invalid domain, which is guaranteed never to resolve.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A one-line configuration change closes the channel — cheap remediation means the persistence of the problem is an attention failure, not a cost failure.
insights.quote: companies could use internal domains or the .invalid domain that is guaranteed not to exist
insights.locator: While the issue is not a new one

insights.claim: Buying a placeholder domain costs about $15 and yields immediate results: Mike Sheward saw three different organizations email sensitive material to deleteduser.com within the first hour of ownership.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: The cost-to-yield ratio is so extreme that assuming adversaries have not already done this is untenable.
insights.quote: Within the first hour, there were three different organizations that had emailed stuff to @deleteduser.com

insights.claim: Solovewicz and Sheward, working independently, have bought more than 30 placeholder domains specifically to keep them out of the hands of hackers and extortionists, a private defensive-squatting effort with no institutional backing.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Critical internet hygiene is being funded out of two researchers' pockets — a fragile arrangement and an argument for registry-level reservation of placeholder namespaces.
insights.locator: As both Solovewicz and Sheward realized the potential scale

insights.claim: Notification of affected organizations has produced mixed results — some quietly fixed the misconfiguration while many never replied — and the volume makes individual disclosure impractical, which is why Solovewicz went public at Defcon instead.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: When one-to-one disclosure breaks down, public conference disclosure becomes the remediation channel — watch Defcon talks as leading indicators of enterprise incident waves.
insights.quote: I’m at the point where this would now be a full-time job to handle every single one of these—that’s part of my motivation to talk about this, it is my responsible disclosure.
insights.locator: Both researchers say that, where possible, they have been notifying companies

insights.claim: The researchers frame the current situation as luck rather than safety: the data landed with benign owners, and equivalent collection by criminals or nation-states would have produced a usable extortion and intrusion goldmine.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Treat any unowned placeholder domain in your mail configuration as an active exfiltration channel, not a null route.
insights.quote: I am being a good guardian of the internet dumpster—but if I had been a bad one, it’s not hard to see how this information that is willingly thrown at my face could be misused
insights.locator: One of the most frequent sources of email
